mx.cwo: The Moon is a planet because it is Earth's nearest neighbour and has a round surface with craters.
A spacecraft sent to study the Moon is Earth's natural satellite just like the Moon.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Moons are natural satellites of planets, and Earth's Moon is Earth's natural satellite; it is smaller than planets, revolves around Earth, has hardly any atmosphere, and is Earth's nearest neighbour in space.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Satellite means any machine sent into space, so the Moon cannot be a satellite.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says the Moon is a satellite without natural status or revolution around Earth.
Uses satellite for every object sent near or around the Moon.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Distinguish asteroids from comets by shape, composition, position, tail, and motion around the Sun.
units.mechanism: Asteroids are small rocky, irregular Solar System objects, many of which revolve around the Sun between Mars and Jupiter; comets are objects made of dust, gases, rocks, and ice that can show long tails as they approach close to the Sun.

mx.cwo: An asteroid is an icy object with a long tail near the Sun, and a comet is a rocky object in the belt between Mars and Jupiter.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Asteroids are small rocky, irregular Solar System objects, many of which revolve around the Sun between Mars and Jupiter; comets are objects made of dust, gases, rocks, and ice that can show long tails as they approach close to the Sun.
pedagogy.lok_folk: All small objects in the Solar System are comets if they move around the Sun.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names asteroid and comet without evidence.
Uses tail to name comet but ignores the rocky belt object.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Organize objects beyond the Solar System into the Milky Way Galaxy, other galaxies, exoplanets, and the still-open question of life elsewhere.
units.mechanism: The Milky Way is our home galaxy and can appear as a faint band of light from a very dark moonless location; beyond it there are many galaxies, and exoplanets are planets discovered revolving around other stars in our galaxy, while life elsewhere in the Universe is not yet known.

mx.cwo: An exoplanet is a planet revolving around the Sun beyond the Milky Way, and finding one proves life exists there.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: The Milky Way is our home galaxy and can appear as a faint band of light from a very dark moonless location; beyond it there are many galaxies, and exoplanets are planets discovered revolving around other stars in our galaxy, while life elsewhere in the Universe is not yet known.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Anything beyond the Solar System is just a far star, so galaxies, exoplanets, and evidence of life are the same idea.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names Milky Way, galaxies, exoplanets, and life without relations.
Uses space terms fluently while saying exoplanets orbit the Sun beyond the Milky Way.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether science in this chapter is being treated as a list of facts to memorise or as a process of curiosity, questioning, experimenting, and exploring patterns.
units.mechanism: Science is presented as a way of thinking: it welcomes curiosity, asks questions, supports experiments, and looks for patterns rather than stopping at facts.

mx.cwo: Science in Grade 7 is just memorising facts like cells are tiny and the Sun moves; asking why is extra.
First collect the facts from the chapter, and only after the facts are complete can curiosity and experiments begin.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner classifies science as an active way of thinking that uses curiosity, questions, experiments, and pattern seeking rather than as only a list of facts.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Science class means memorising textbook facts and correct answers; questions and experiments are interesting extras.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names facts or topics and says science has correct answers.
Mentions experiments but only after all facts are learned.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether learning science should stay inside the book or extend into observing, doing activities, and experimenting with the world around you.
units.mechanism: The chapter presents science learning as something that moves beyond reading: learners step out of the book and classroom through activities, experiments, observations, and careful thinking.

mx.cwo: Reading the paragraph is enough; I do not need to observe anything or do the experiment.
For the activity, I will underline the words activities and experiments and then close the book.
Experiments matter only after the book has already given the full understanding; observations do not build understanding.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner applies the chapter's view that science learning moves beyond reading into observations, activities, experiments, and careful thinking.
pedagogy.lok_folk: If I read the book and know the topic name, I have learned the science; observing and experimenting are optional fun.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says 'activities and experiments' without a learning move.
Says reading plus activity but gives no observation, question, or thinking.
Mentions experiments but says they only check what the book already completed.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether the different fields and chapters of science should be treated as isolated subjects or as connected ways of studying the same world.
units.mechanism: The chapter says science includes fields such as physics, chemistry, biology, and earth sciences, but these fields are connected even when they appear in different chapters.

mx.cwo: Physics, chemistry, biology, and earth science are separate chapters, so light cannot help us ask about eclipses or the Sun.
This part is only about sour fruits and haldi stains because those examples are named first.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner compares science fields as connected parts of one scientific journey, using examples such as materials, body changes, light, shadows, eclipses, and day-night patterns.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Each chapter belongs to a separate subject box, so physics, chemistry, biology, and earth science should be learned without connecting them.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Lists physics, chemistry, biology, and earth sciences.
Mentions sour fruits or haldi stains.
Says fields are in different chapters.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a valid scientific question can be formed from a given answer by inventing a curious situation, instead of only asking the most obvious matching question.
units.mechanism: To think like a scientist, it is important to ask interesting questions; in the activity, many curious and creative questions can lead to the same given answer.

mx.cwo: Question for answer 42: What is 32+10?
The answer 42 cannot come first; there must already be one correct question before I can answer it.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner applies the activity rule by inventing a curious, creative question or situation that sensibly leads to the given answer.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A school task always has one question and one answer, so the learner should recover the teacher's expected question instead of inventing a curious one.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Matches answer 42 with What is 32+10?.
Says one correct question must already exist.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Classify a substance as acidic, basic, or neutral from paired blue-litmus and red-litmus responses.
units.mechanism: Acidic samples make blue litmus red; basic samples make red litmus blue; neutral samples leave both litmus papers unchanged.

mx.cwo: Salt solution is called acidic because red litmus did not change.
Lemon juice is called basic because blue litmus became red.
Tap water is called acidic because a litmus strip looks different after a messy drop.

pedagogy.lok_folk: student says litmus paper just shows a colour but cannot say which observation decides acid or base

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: May pass items where one changing strip is enough.
May notice a colour change but attach the wrong nature.
May choose a label from any visible difference.

pedagogy.anti_narration: hide the response mapping; require the learner to choose which observation decides the label

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Use natural acid-base indicators to infer the nature of an unknown substance from colour changes.
units.mechanism: A prepared natural indicator gives a response pattern in acidic or basic media, so the observed colour after adding a sample is evidence for the sample's nature.

mx.cwo: Red rose extract is called the acid because it turns red with lemon juice.
Soap solution is called acidic because the rose petals started red.
Turmeric paper should turn green with soap solution because rose extract does.

pedagogy.lok_folk: student says flowers are used because they are colourful but gives no link between rose extract and lemon or soap tests

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: chooses red rose extract as the acid when lemon juice is shown
uses red petal colour to call soap solution acidic
says turmeric paper turns green with soap because rose extract does

pedagogy.anti_narration: show an observed colour change without naming the medium type

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Connect common acidic substances with sour taste and named food acids while preserving the safety rule against tasting unknown substances.
units.mechanism: Several edible sour substances contain acids, but unknown substances must not be tasted because taste is not a safe identification method.

mx.cwo: An unknown vinegar-smelling liquid should be tasted to prove it is acidic.
Curd is not acidic because it does not look like lemon juice.

pedagogy.lok_folk: student remembers that lemon tastes sour but cannot explain acid names or the rule against tasting unknown samples

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Mentions sour taste or vinegar smell without checking whether the sample is unknown.
Calls lemon acidic but rejects another food by appearance.

pedagogy.anti_narration: do not reveal whether taste is allowed; ask which evidence is safe

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Identify common basic substances using slippery feel and indicator evidence while avoiding the bitter-equals-base shortcut.
units.mechanism: Basic substances such as baking soda solution may feel slippery and turn red litmus blue, but bitter taste alone does not prove that a substance is basic.

mx.cwo: Bitter gourd is basic because it tastes bitter.
Lemon juice is basic because it feels wet like soap solution.

pedagogy.lok_folk: student names baking soda or soap but cannot tell which observation would show basic nature

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: labels a bitter item as basic without testing evidence
treats wet lemon juice as basic like soap solution

pedagogy.anti_narration: ask for evidence without stating the red-litmus response

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Judge the diagnostic limits of turmeric paper as an indicator for acids, bases, and neutral substances.
units.mechanism: Turmeric paper detects basic substances by a colour change but cannot separate acidic substances from neutral substances when both give no change.

mx.cwo: Vinegar is neutral because turmeric paper does not change.
Sugar solution and vinegar are definitely the same because both leave turmeric yellow.
Baking soda solution is acidic because turmeric paper changes colour.

pedagogy.lok_folk: student says turmeric is an indicator but cannot state which kind of sample it can and cannot distinguish

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Cites no change on turmeric but turns it into a neutral label.
Compares vinegar and sugar solution by their shared turmeric result.
Uses colour change as a deciding observation.

pedagogy.anti_narration: present turmeric results without naming which group is directly detected

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Design and interpret a fair natural-indicator test using prepared extracts or indicator papers.
units.mechanism: A fair indicator comparison uses the same prepared indicator, comparable sample amounts, and recorded final colours so differences are due to sample nature rather than procedure.

mx.cwo: Use rose extract for lemon juice but turmeric paper for soap solution, then compare colours directly.
Add twenty drops of lemon juice and one drop of soap solution, then decide which is stronger.

pedagogy.lok_folk: student can list materials like petals and droppers but cannot say why the same procedure is needed

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: says to compare colour changes but hides a switch between rose extract and turmeric paper
says to use droppers but leaves the sample amounts unmatched

pedagogy.anti_narration: ask about procedure choices without stating the control variable

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Select an olfactory indicator when colour-based indicators are unsuitable for the observer or task.
units.mechanism: Olfactory indicators provide evidence through a change in odour in acidic or basic media, so they can support testing when visual colour evidence is unsuitable.

mx.cwo: Onion strips are colour indicators because olfactory means coloured.
A blindfolded student should use red litmus paper because all indicators must be seen.

pedagogy.lok_folk: student repeats the word olfactory but cannot connect it to onion strips or odour change

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: says olfactory indicator without naming odour change
uses onion strips but says olfactory means coloured
chooses red litmus because it is a known indicator

pedagogy.anti_narration: do not announce the sensory channel; require selection from task constraints

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Explain neutralisation as sufficient mixing of an acid and a base to form a solution that is neither acidic nor basic.
units.mechanism: When enough base is added to an acid, or enough acid to a base, the resulting solution can become neither acidic nor basic while salt, water, and heat are produced.

mx.cwo: Lime water only waters down lemon juice, so no new salt or heat idea is involved.
One tiny drop of lime water must fully neutralise any amount of lemon juice.
Adding extra lemon juice to an acidic tube should make it basic.

pedagogy.lok_folk: student says colours changed in the test tube but cannot explain why lime water changes the lemon-juice result

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: says neutralised without evidence
mentions red to blue but gives a dilution story
names lime water as base but skips amount

pedagogy.anti_narration: show the sequence of additions without naming the process or products

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Apply neutralisation reasoning to ant bites, acidic or basic soil, and factory waste in water.
units.mechanism: A remedy should oppose the original acidic or basic condition: a base can reduce an acidic ant bite or acidic soil, while acid-releasing organic matter can reduce basic soil.

mx.cwo: Acidic soil should be treated with vinegar because vinegar is also acidic.
The farmer should add lemon juice because lime sounds like the fruit lime.
Neutral soil must be treated with baking soda whenever plants look unhealthy.

pedagogy.lok_folk: student remembers ant bite and soil examples but cannot infer which nature the remedy must oppose

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Uses acidic soil and vinegar together because both are acidic.
Says lime but means lemon juice or fruit lime.
Chooses baking soda whenever plants look unhealthy.

pedagogy.anti_narration: give the situation and possible remedies without naming which one opposes the condition

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Justify an acid-base classification from a multi-indicator evidence table.
units.mechanism: A classification is justified by combining all indicator observations so that the accepted label fits every row and the rejected labels conflict with at least one row.

mx.cwo: The liquid sample is neutral because red litmus has no change.
The liquid sample is basic because the turmeric row is easiest to notice.
The table proves acid because it has three observations, even without checking alternatives.

pedagogy.lok_folk: student can copy the table rows but cannot combine red litmus, blue litmus, and turmeric into one justified label

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: neutral because red litmus has no change
basic because the turmeric row is easiest to notice
acid because the table has three observations

pedagogy.anti_narration: provide the table but require the learner to choose the deciding combination

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide which end of an electric cell is the positive terminal, which is the negative terminal, and why the cell can run a small circuit.
units.mechanism: An electric cell is a portable source of electrical energy with two terminals: the metal cap is positive and the metal disc is negative.

mx.cwo: The flat metal disc is the positive terminal and the protruding metal cap is the negative terminal.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: An electric cell is a portable source of electrical energy with two terminals: the metal cap is positive and the metal disc is negative.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Either end of a cell can be called positive if the + mark is not noticed; cap and disc shape do not matter.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Mentions positive and negative terminals without assigning cap and disc signs.
Uses terminal words but may give the disc-positive, cap-negative output.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether two or more cells have been placed to make a working battery for a device.
units.mechanism: A working battery connects the positive terminal of one cell to the negative terminal of the next; more than one cell can give a circuit energy for a longer time and/or more energy.

mx.cwo: The two-cell torch battery will work when the positive terminal of one cell touches the positive terminal of the next cell.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: A working battery connects the positive terminal of one cell to the negative terminal of the next; more than one cell can give a circuit energy for a longer time and/or more energy.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Putting two cells anywhere in the holder makes a battery; terminal order is only for neat placement.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says two cells make a battery.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether an incandescent torch lamp can glow by checking its filament.
units.mechanism: In an incandescent electric lamp, the thin wire inside the glass bulb is the filament that glows; if the filament is broken, the lamp is fused and will not glow.

mx.cwo: The two thick support wires are the filament, so a lamp with the thin middle wire broken will still glow.
A fused lamp with a broken filament will glow when connected to a cell because the break lets current pass.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: In an incandescent electric lamp, the thin wire inside the glass bulb is the filament that glows; if the filament is broken, the lamp is fused and will not glow.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A torch lamp glows if the outside glass bulb looks whole; the filament is just a visible detail.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says filament and no glow but gives no broken-filament reason.
Identifies an internal wire but may mean support wires.
Predicts glow or no glow without naming the filament condition.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a cell and lamp arrangement makes the lamp glow.
units.mechanism: The lamp glows when one terminal of the lamp is connected to one terminal of the electric cell and the other terminal of the lamp is connected to the other terminal of the cell, forming a complete electrical circuit.

mx.cwo: The lamp will stay off when one lamp terminal is connected to the cell positive terminal and the other lamp terminal is connected to the cell negative terminal.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: The lamp glows when one terminal of the lamp is connected to one terminal of the electric cell and the other terminal of the lamp is connected to the other terminal of the cell, forming a complete electrical circuit.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A lamp will glow whenever any wire touches the cell and the lamp, even without a complete path between both terminals.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says yes without showing the terminal path.
Says complete circuit but ignores both lamp terminals.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether an LED connection will make the LED glow.
units.mechanism: An LED has no filament and allows current to pass through it in one direction only; it glows when its positive terminal is connected to the positive side of the battery and its negative terminal is connected to the negative side.

mx.cwo: The LED will glow when its longer wire is connected to the negative battery terminal and its shorter wire is connected to the positive battery terminal.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: An LED has no filament and allows current to pass through it in one direction only; it glows when its positive terminal is connected to the positive side of the battery and its negative terminal is connected to the negative side.
pedagogy.lok_folk: An LED is just a small lamp, so either connection direction works.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Mentions positive and negative terminals without matching LED wires to battery sides.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a switch is making a circuit ON or OFF.
units.mechanism: A switch is a simple device that completes or breaks a circuit; when the switch closes the gap, the circuit is ON and current flows, and when it breaks the path, the circuit is OFF.

mx.cwo: The switch is OFF when the safety pin touches both drawing pins and ON when the safety pin leaves a gap.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: A switch is a simple device that completes or breaks a circuit; when the switch closes the gap, the circuit is ON and current flows, and when it breaks the path, the circuit is OFF.
pedagogy.lok_folk: The switch itself supplies current, so sliding it tells the lamp to turn on or off.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Gives the right ON/OFF word for one case without using the gap or path.
Says the lamp glows after switch movement but claims the switch gives current.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide how to translate an actual circuit into a circuit diagram.
units.mechanism: Electrical components can be represented by standard symbols, and a circuit diagram is a representation of an electrical circuit using those symbols.

mx.cwo: The Fig. 3.10c LED circuit diagram can show a battery and LED symbol but leave the LED negative terminal unconnected.
In a cell symbol, the short line is the positive terminal and the long line is the negative terminal.
A correct circuit diagram is a drawing of the red cell, yellow LED, and wires exactly as they look, without standard symbols.
Use the circle-with-X lamp symbol for the LED in the Fig. 3.10c circuit diagram.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Electrical components can be represented by standard symbols, and a circuit diagram is a representation of an electrical circuit using those symbols.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A circuit diagram is any neat picture of the parts, so exact symbols and terminal orientation are optional.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names battery and LED without proving the actual connections.
Adds + and - labels without using the long-line and short-line rule.
Produces a tidy drawing of the red cell, yellow LED, and wires.
Names LED but draws the lamp symbol.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a material placed in a circuit will let the lamp glow.
units.mechanism: Conductors allow electric current to pass easily through them, while insulators do not; metals are conductors, and plastic, rubber, and ceramics are insulators.

mx.cwo: A plastic scale connected between A and B will make the lamp glow, while a metal key will not.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Conductors allow electric current to pass easily through them, while insulators do not; metals are conductors, and plastic, rubber, and ceramics are insulators.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Any solid object touching both free wire ends should let electricity pass and make the lamp glow.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names conductor or insulator without tying it to lamp glow.
Gets the metal case right while leaving the plastic-scale reversal untested.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide when an electrical situation is unsafe to handle.
units.mechanism: Electricity can be dangerous if it is not handled carefully, and the human body conducts electricity; current through the body may cause severe injury or death.

mx.cwo: It is safe to touch a switch or plug with wet hands because the human body does not conduct electricity.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Electricity can be dangerous if it is not handled carefully, and the human body conducts electricity; current through the body may cause severe injury or death.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Briefly touching household switches or plugs is safe if the person is careful.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Calls wet handling safe by claiming the body does not conduct electricity.

units.subject: science
units.chapter_title: The world of metals and non-metals
units.decision_hinge: When a material is observed, decide whether its lustre, hardness, malleability, ductility, sonority, and conductivity point to a metal or to a non-metal, while allowing named exceptions.
units.mechanism: Metals are generally lustrous, hard, malleable, ductile, sonorous, and good conductors of heat and electricity; most non-metals lack these properties. Sodium and potassium are soft metals, and mercury is a liquid metal at room temperature.

mx.cwo: Mercury is a non-metal because it is liquid at room temperature.
Coal is a metal because it is non-lustrous and not as hard as copper, aluminium, or iron.
Sodium and potassium are non-metals because all metals must be hard solids.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Metals are generally lustrous, hard, malleable, ductile, sonorous, and good conductors of heat and electricity; most non-metals lack these properties. Sodium and potassium are soft metals, and mercury is a liquid metal at room temperature.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Metals are always hard, shiny solids, so anything soft or liquid is a non-metal.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Gives metal or non-metal labels without evidence.
Names mercury, sodium, or potassium without applying the class decision.
Mentions lustre or hardness but maps coal-like evidence to metal.

units.subject: science
units.chapter_title: The world of metals and non-metals
units.decision_hinge: When a hammered sample flattens, breaks, or does neither, decide whether it is malleable, brittle, or neither.
units.mechanism: Copper, iron, and aluminium flatten into sheets when beaten; this flattening property is malleability. Coal and sulfur break into pieces and are brittle, while wood neither flattens into a sheet nor breaks into pieces in this comparison.

mx.cwo: Coal is malleable because it breaks into pieces when hammered.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Copper, iron, and aluminium flatten into sheets when beaten; this flattening property is malleability. Coal and sulfur break into pieces and are brittle, while wood neither flattens into a sheet nor breaks into pieces in this comparison.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Hammered materials have only two outcomes: metals flatten and everything else is brittle.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: names copper malleable and coal brittle without saying what hammering showed
uses chapter words but says breaking proves malleability

units.subject: science
units.chapter_title: The world of metals and non-metals
units.decision_hinge: When a material must be drawn into wire, decide whether ductility makes a metal such as copper, aluminium, or steel suitable and coal or sulfur unsuitable.
units.mechanism: Ductility is the property by which materials can be drawn into wires, and it is mainly possessed by metals. Copper, aluminium, and steel can be used as wires, while coal and sulfur are not ductile.

mx.cwo: Coal can be used for making wire because it is a hard solid.
Copper is unsuitable for making wires because it can be drawn into wires.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Ductility is the property by which materials can be drawn into wires, and it is mainly possessed by metals. Copper, aluminium, and steel can be used as wires, while coal and sulfur are not ductile.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Any strong or hard solid can be made into wire if enough force is used.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Chooses copper but gives no ductility or wire-drawing reason.
Says a hard or strong material should make wire.

units.subject: science
units.chapter_title: The world of metals and non-metals
units.decision_hinge: When objects are dropped or struck, decide from their sound whether the material is sonorous.
units.mechanism: Metals such as a spoon or coin produce a ringing sound, while coal and wood produce dull sounds. The property of metals that enables a ringing sound is sonority.

mx.cwo: Wood is sonorous because it produces a dull sound when struck.
Coal is sonorous because every solid object makes some sound when dropped.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Metals such as a spoon or coin produce a ringing sound, while coal and wood produce dull sounds. The property of metals that enables a ringing sound is sonority.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Sonorous means an object makes any sound at all when hit.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names spoon or coin as sonorous without saying ringing sound.
Says all dropped objects make sound, so all are sonorous.
Calls wood sonorous from dull sound.

units.subject: science
units.chapter_title: The world of metals and non-metals
units.decision_hinge: When choosing materials for heating water or making handles, decide whether heat conduction makes a material suitable or unsafe.
units.mechanism: Conduction is the transfer of heat from one point to another in a material. Metals transfer heat well, so metal spoons get hotter than wooden spoons in the same hot water and metal vessels are used for cooking; wood and plastic are poor conductors and are suitable for handles.

mx.cwo: Use wood for the cooking vessel because it stays cooler than a metal spoon in hot water.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Conduction is the transfer of heat from one point to another in a material. Metals transfer heat well, so metal spoons get hotter than wooden spoons in the same hot water and metal vessels are used for cooking; wood and plastic are poor conductors and are suitable for handles.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A good cooking material should be used for every part of the utensil, including the handle.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says wood stays cooler than metal in hot water.

units.subject: science
units.chapter_title: The world of metals and non-metals
units.decision_hinge: When a circuit tester is used, decide from bulb glow whether a material conducts electricity and how that affects electrical safety.
units.mechanism: Materials that allow electricity to flow through them easily are good conductors and make the bulb glow; materials that do not allow electricity to pass through them are poor conductors and prevent the bulb from glowing. Aluminium, iron, and copper conduct in the tester, while sulfur, coal, wood, stone, rubber eraser, and nylon rope do not.

mx.cwo: If the bulb does not glow when testing nylon rope in an incomplete circuit, nylon must be a poor conductor.
Sulfur is a good conductor because the bulb does not glow.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Materials that allow electricity to flow through them easily are good conductors and make the bulb glow; materials that do not allow electricity to pass through them are poor conductors and prevent the bulb from glowing. Aluminium, iron, and copper conduct in the tester, while sulfur, coal, wood, stone, rubber eraser, and nylon rope do not.
pedagogy.lok_folk: The tester bulb result mainly tells whether the bulb works, not what the material does to electricity.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Calls nylon rope a poor conductor from no glow.
Uses the terms glow, no glow, and conductor in one answer.
Lists some correct material labels without explaining bulb glow or safety.

units.subject: science
units.chapter_title: The world of metals and non-metals
units.decision_hinge: For an iron object, decide whether rusting needs contact with both air and water and how to prevent it.
units.mechanism: Iron develops brown deposits only when it is in contact with both air and water. Dry air without water and water shielded from air do not produce brown deposits; rusting can be prevented by painting, oiling, greasing, or applying zinc on iron.

mx.cwo: An iron nail in dry air will form brown rust because air touches it.
Painting an iron gate makes it rust because the paint keeps air and water on the iron.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Iron develops brown deposits only when it is in contact with both air and water. Dry air without water and water shielded from air do not produce brown deposits; rusting can be prevented by painting, oiling, greasing, or applying zinc on iron.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Iron rusts when it touches either air or water; one of them is enough.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names air and rust but skips the water condition.
Names paint or oil but gives no contact-blocking mechanism.

units.subject: science
units.chapter_title: The world of metals and non-metals
units.decision_hinge: When magnesium or sulfur burns in air and the product is tested with water and litmus, decide whether the product is basic or acidic.
units.mechanism: Burning magnesium in oxygen forms magnesium oxide, a white powder that turns red litmus blue and is basic; generally, oxides of metals are basic. Burning sulfur in oxygen forms sulfur dioxide, which dissolves in water to form sulfurous acid, so the resulting solution is acidic.

mx.cwo: Burning sulfur proves the product solution is acidic even without dissolving the gas in water.
Test unburnt magnesium ribbon and sulfur powder with litmus to decide whether their burning products are basic or acidic.
Magnesium oxide is acidic because it turns red litmus blue, while sulfur dioxide solution is basic.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Burning magnesium in oxygen forms magnesium oxide, a white powder that turns red litmus blue and is basic; generally, oxides of metals are basic. Burning sulfur in oxygen forms sulfur dioxide, which dissolves in water to form sulfurous acid, so the resulting solution is acidic.
pedagogy.lok_folk: All products made by burning in air are acidic because burning makes smoke or ash.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Gives basic for magnesium and acidic for sulfur without naming products or tests.
Says sulfur is acidic but hides whether sulfur dioxide dissolved in water.
Mentions red litmus and blue but may reverse acidic and basic meanings.

units.subject: science
units.chapter_title: The world of metals and non-metals
units.decision_hinge: When a substance is exposed to air or water, decide whether it must be stored away from one of them because of its reactivity.
units.mechanism: Sodium is a metal stored in kerosene because it reacts vigorously with oxygen and water and produces much heat. Phosphorus is stored in water because it catches fire when exposed to atmospheric air, while sulfur placed in water shows no reaction.

mx.cwo: Sodium should be stored in water because water prevents sodium from reacting.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Sodium is a metal stored in kerosene because it reacts vigorously with oxygen and water and produces much heat. Phosphorus is stored in water because it catches fire when exposed to atmospheric air, while sulfur placed in water shows no reaction.
pedagogy.lok_folk: All reactive substances need the same storage liquid; the liquid just keeps them covered.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names a storage medium for a named substance.

units.subject: science
units.chapter_title: The world of metals and non-metals
units.decision_hinge: When sorting substances and materials, decide whether something is an element classified as a metal or non-metal or an everyday material that is not in either class.
units.mechanism: Metals and non-metals are sub-categories of elements, and an element cannot be broken down into simpler substances. Oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, and carbon are non-metals; plastic, glass, wood, rubber, and paper are materials that are not classified as metals or non-metals.

mx.cwo: Plastic is a non-metal element because it is not shiny and does not conduct electricity like metals.
Oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, and carbon are not elements because they are non-metals.
Wood, rubber, paper, plastic, and glass are non-metals because they are not metals.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Metals and non-metals are sub-categories of elements, and an element cannot be broken down into simpler substances. Oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, and carbon are non-metals; plastic, glass, wood, rubber, and paper are materials that are not classified as metals or non-metals.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Anything that is not a metal should be placed in the non-metal category.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: places oxygen and carbon in the non-metal column
labels materials as non-metals with confident language

units.subject: science
units.chapter_title: The world of metals and non-metals
units.decision_hinge: When explaining everyday importance, decide that non-metals are essential even though many metals are visible in tools and technologies.
units.mechanism: Non-metals have important uses: oxygen is needed for breathing and survival, carbon is a building block of life forms and key components needed for growth and energy, nitrogen is used in fertilisers and supports plant growth, and chlorine is used in water purification.

mx.cwo: Nitrogen is not important for plants because plants need soil, not fertilisers.
Non-metals are not essential because metals are the materials seen in tools, utensils, and technologies.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Non-metals have important uses: oxygen is needed for breathing and survival, carbon is a building block of life forms and key components needed for growth and energy, nitrogen is used in fertilisers and supports plant growth, and chlorine is used in water purification.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Useful substances are mainly visible metals in tools, so gases and less visible non-metals do not count as important.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Mentions plants but avoids nitrogen's fertiliser role.
Lists metal tools or technologies as everyday evidence.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a change is physical or chemical by checking whether a new substance has formed.
units.mechanism: A physical change changes physical properties while no new substance is formed; a chemical change forms one or more new substances.

mx.cwo: Folding paper into a boat is a chemical change because the paper has a new shape.
Rusting of iron is a physical change because a brown substance called rust is formed.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner classifies a change by checking whether the material remains the same or whether one or more new substances are formed.
pedagogy.lok_folk: If an object looks different after a change, the change must be chemical.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Chooses physical or chemical without before/after material evidence.
Mentions changed shape, size, bubbles, or rust without mapping to substance formation.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide when lime water turning milky is evidence for carbon dioxide and a chemical change.
units.mechanism: Carbon dioxide turns lime water milky because calcium hydroxide reacts with carbon dioxide to form insoluble calcium carbonate and water.

mx.cwo: The gas from vinegar and baking soda is carbon dioxide because the test tube fizzes, even without passing the gas through lime water.
Lime water turns milky because calcium carbonate changes into carbon dioxide and calcium hydroxide.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner explains that carbon dioxide turns lime water milky because it reacts with calcium hydroxide to form insoluble calcium carbonate and water.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Any fizzing bubbles from a mixture are carbon dioxide, whether or not lime water turns milky.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names carbon dioxide without the lime-water condition.
Mentions calcium carbonate and carbon dioxide but reverses their roles.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a reaction is combustion by checking for reaction with oxygen and production of heat or light.
units.mechanism: Combustion is a chemical reaction in which a substance reacts with oxygen and produces heat or light.

mx.cwo: Burning magnesium is combustion because magnesium oxide produces oxygen, heat, and light.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner classifies combustion by checking that a substance reacts with oxygen and produces heat or light.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Combustion just means a flame or bright light appears, so oxygen reaction does not need to be checked.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says burning magnesium is combustion because heat or light appears.
Names magnesium oxide, oxygen, heat, and light.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Predict whether combustion will start or continue by checking for fuel, oxygen, and enough heat to reach ignition temperature.
units.mechanism: Combustion requires a combustible substance, oxygen, and heat that lets the fuel reach its ignition temperature.

mx.cwo: A candle covered by a glass tumbler will keep burning because wax is fuel and the flame is already hot.
Wrapping a burning cloth with a blanket makes the fire stronger because the blanket supplies the air needed for burning.
A sheet of paper kept in air will catch fire by itself because paper is combustible and oxygen is present.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner predicts burning by checking all three requirements: fuel, oxygen, and enough heat to reach ignition temperature.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A fire burns as long as there is fuel; oxygen and ignition temperature are optional details.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Mentions wax fuel and flame heat for the covered candle.
Uses blanket as the key object but not its air-cutoff effect.
Correctly names paper as fuel and air as present.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide when one process includes both physical and chemical changes.
units.mechanism: A single process can include physical changes and chemical changes when some parts only change state while another part forms new substances.

mx.cwo: Burning a candle is only a physical change because the wax melts and later solidifies.
Wax vapour first burns to make new substances, and that burning then causes the solid wax to melt and move up the wick.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner identifies that a burning candle includes physical changes in wax and a chemical change when wax vapour burns to form new substances.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A process must be either physical or chemical, so a burning candle cannot be both.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Mentions wax melting or solidifying and sounds chapter-based.
Says both physical and chemical changes occur in a candle.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a change is reversible by asking whether the original object or substance can be brought back.
units.mechanism: A change is reversible when the original object or substance can be brought back in the form it started with.

mx.cwo: Melting ice is irreversible because melted water can be refrozen into ice.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner classifies a change as reversible only when the original object or substance can be brought back in its starting form.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Once something changes, it is permanent unless it simply looks unchanged by itself.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Mentions refreezing melted water but chooses irreversible.
Says chopped pieces are still vegetables, so the change can be undone.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a change is desirable or undesirable by using the situation and purpose, not the change name alone.
units.mechanism: A change is desirable when it is useful in a situation and undesirable when it is harmful or unwanted in that situation.

mx.cwo: Decay of stored food is desirable because decomposition of food waste can make compost in another situation.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner judges desirable or undesirable change by the usefulness, harm, or purpose in the stated situation.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A change has one fixed value label, so the same kind of change is always desirable or always undesirable.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Mentions compost usefulness when asked about decay.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether slow natural changes in rocks and soil are physical or chemical by checking what natural forces do to the materials.
units.mechanism: Natural factors can break down and move rocks, soil, and sediments; use the new-substance test to decide whether the change is physical or chemical.

mx.cwo: Erosion during a landslide is a chemical change because rock pebbles are broken down and moved by flowing water.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner explains slow natural changes by identifying what natural forces do and then using the new-substance test for physical or chemical classification.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Slow natural changes in rocks are chemical because they happen over many years.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: answers physical or chemical without explaining the force effect
mentions erosion or landslide but keeps the chemical wrong output

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a learner is describing adolescence as the human stage between childhood and adulthood, generally from about 10 to 19 years, when growth and reproductive maturity develop.
units.mechanism: Adolescence is the period of change from childhood to adulthood. It generally begins around 10 years of age and usually lasts until 19 years, and the body gradually reaches maturity for reproduction during this period.

mx.cwo: A tall 9-year-old who has gained weight is already in adolescence because height and weight changed.
A child first becomes reproductively mature, and that maturity is what starts adolescence at age 10.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner identifies adolescence as the human period between childhood and adulthood, generally around ages 10 to 19, during which growth and reproductive maturity develop.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Adolescence just means getting taller around middle school age.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says yes, it is adolescence.
Uses height or weight change as proof.
Mentions reproduction but not the order.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether common visible changes such as increased height, broader shoulders, wider chest, pimples, hoarse voice, or new body hair are normal adolescent changes rather than identical changes for every person.
units.mechanism: During adolescence, visible body changes can include increased height, changes in body structure, weight gain, greater strength, voice changes, acne, and new hair in parts of the body. The timing, nature, and extent of these changes vary among individuals and this variation is normal.

mx.cwo: Every 12-year-old should have pimples, new armpit hair, and a hoarse voice if adolescence is normal.
A thin moustache is a normal adolescent change, but pimples and a wider chest are not part of adolescence.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner classifies visible changes such as height, body structure, voice, pimples, and body hair as normal adolescent changes while preserving individual variation.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Adolescent change means the same obvious body changes happen to every student in the same grade.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says the claim is wrong but gives no variation condition.
Mentions moustache or hair as normal and ignores pimples or wider chest.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a physical feature is a secondary sexual characteristic that marks the onset of puberty and shows that the body is preparing for adulthood.
units.mechanism: Secondary sexual characteristics are natural signs that the body is preparing for adulthood and they mark the onset of puberty. Puberty includes external and internal changes during adolescence.

mx.cwo: A boy's facial hair means he is already an adult, so puberty happened after adulthood began.
Only facial hair and breast development count in puberty; maturation of reproductive parts is not part of puberty.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner classifies features such as voice change, facial hair, chest hair, and breast development as secondary sexual characteristics that mark puberty and preparation for adulthood.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Puberty is just any visible body change that makes someone look older.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names secondary sexual characteristics but gives no puberty-marker meaning.
Uses facial hair or breast development but says it proves the person is already adult.
Lists visible signs while omitting internal reproductive changes.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether menstruation should be understood as a natural adolescent body process linked with reproductive maturation, not as a reason for fear, shame, guilt, or taboo.
units.mechanism: An important internal change in adolescent girls is the onset of the menstrual cycle. Wrong beliefs about menstruation can create unnecessary fear, shame, guilt, myths, and taboos, so menstruation should be understood as a natural body process.

mx.cwo: A girl menstruates because she has done something shameful, so she should be physically isolated during her period.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner explains menstruation as a natural adolescent body process linked with reproductive maturation and rejects fear, shame, guilt, myths, and taboos as biological explanations.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Periods are a shameful social problem, not a normal body process.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: says menstruation is natural but gives no menstrual-cycle link or taboo rejection
uses caring language while still accepting guilt or physical isolation

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether adolescence includes emotional and behavioural changes in addition to physical changes, and whether recognising emotions can help a person choose thoughtful actions.
units.mechanism: Adolescence is not only about physical and reproductive changes. It is also marked by emotional and behavioural changes, with stronger emotions than childhood that can affect behaviour and actions; understanding this influence helps people make better choices.

mx.cwo: Adolescence brings only taller height, body hair, and pimples; mood swings are unrelated to this age.
If an adolescent feels sudden anger, the anger should decide the action and thinking about it cannot change the response.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner applies the idea that adolescence includes emotional and behavioural changes as well as physical changes, and that recognizing emotions can guide thoughtful action.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Adolescence is only about body changes, and feelings are separate personal issues.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Mentions mood swings or emotions without revising the physical-only claim.
Says emotions are strong but gives no role for thoughtful choice.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether an adolescent's healthy growth plan should include nutritious food and regular physical activity rather than only one kind of food or no exercise.
units.mechanism: Because adolescence is a period of growth and development marked by several body changes, adolescents need a nutritious diet with proteins, carbohydrates, adequate fats, vitamins, and minerals, along with regular exercise and physical activities.

mx.cwo: Eating only paneer every day is a complete adolescent health plan because paneer has protein and fat; exercise is not needed.
Playing football for two hours means the body no longer needs proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins, or minerals.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner applies the need for a nutritious adolescent diet containing several nutrient groups along with regular exercise and physical activity.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A growing adolescent only needs a favorite filling food; exercise or nutrient variety is optional.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Mentions paneer, protein, or fat.
Mentions football or long exercise.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether personal hygiene, menstrual hygiene, and proper disposal of used sanitary pads are health practices that protect both the body and the community environment.
units.mechanism: Personal hygiene is crucial during adolescence, especially in the armpits and pubic region, because it may protect from potential infections. Proper menstrual hygiene supports comfort and health, and used sanitary pads should be wrapped and put inside a dustbin to support community health and environmental cleanliness.

mx.cwo: Used sanitary pads left beside the bin keep the toilet cleaner because everyone can see them and avoid touching them.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner applies personal hygiene, menstrual hygiene, and proper wrapped dustbin disposal of used sanitary pads as practices that support body comfort, health, community health, and cleanliness.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Hygiene during adolescence just means looking neat; disposal of used pads is someone else's problem.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says hygiene matters without saying what to do with used sanitary pads.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether respectful interaction and responsible social media behaviour are part of a balanced social life during adolescence.
units.mechanism: A balanced social life requires polite and respectful interaction with others. During adolescence, new experiences and emotions make it important to be thoughtful and responsible in person and on social media, including avoiding harmful online actions such as misleading messages, false rumours, and sharing personal information without consent.

mx.cwo: It is responsible online behaviour to write kind comments but share a classmate's photo with a virtual friend if the post is funny.
Spreading a false rumour online creates a safe social environment because it gets attention quickly.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner applies respectful interaction and responsible online behaviour as parts of a balanced social life during adolescence.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Online behaviour is not part of real social life, so posts and rumours do not need the same respect as face-to-face interaction.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names balanced social life or respect without checking online responsibility.
Uses kind language but ignores consent before posting or sharing.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether tobacco, gutka, cigarettes, beedi, alcohol, and illegal drugs should be refused from the first offer because they are harmful and addictive.
units.mechanism: Harmful substances such as tobacco, gutka, cigarettes, beedi, alcohol, and illegal drugs can damage physical and mental health and are addictive. A person should say no to addictive substances the first time and every time, and seek help from trusted people, counselling, or medical advice when needed.

mx.cwo: Trying one cigarette first makes it easier to say no later because addiction only happens after many planned uses.
Only illegal drugs are harmful; tobacco, gutka, beedi, cigarettes, and alcohol are acceptable to try once.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner applies the rule that tobacco, gutka, cigarettes, beedi, alcohol, and illegal drugs should be refused from the first offer because they are harmful and addictive, and help should be sought when needed.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Trying a harmful substance once is a normal adolescent experiment and can always be stopped easily.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says 'say no' without naming the substance or addiction relation.
Correctly refuses illegal drugs but permits gutka, beedi, tobacco, cigarettes, or alcohol.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether many adolescent changes, including menstruation and other signs of puberty, are mainly caused and regulated by hormones produced in the body.
units.mechanism: Many changes in adolescence, including menstruation and other signs of puberty, are mainly due to hormones, which are chemicals produced in the body. Hormones regulate various aspects of growth during adolescence.

mx.cwo: Menstruation and voice change produce hormones; hormones are the result, not the cause, of puberty changes.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner explains many adolescent changes, including menstruation and other signs of puberty, as mainly due to hormones produced in the body that regulate growth and development.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Hormones are just feelings or outside influences that appear after puberty changes happen.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says hormones without explaining causal direction or body-produced chemical meaning.
Mentions hormones and puberty changes but leaves which causes which unclear.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: When one end of a solid metal strip is heated, decide that heat moves along the strip from the hot end to colder parts by conduction, so pins fall in order from nearest to farthest from the flame.
units.mechanism: In conduction through a solid, one particle receives heat and transfers heat to the next particle in contact, while the particles themselves do not move away from their positions.

mx.cwo: Pins I, II, III, and IV all fall at the same time when the candle heats one end of the metal strip.
Pin IV falls first, then pin III, then pin II, and pin I falls last.
The heated metal strip transfers heat by convection because heat moves from one place to another in any medium.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: In conduction through a solid, one particle receives heat and transfers heat to the next particle in contact, while the particles themselves do not move away from their positions.
pedagogy.lok_folk: The flame makes every part of the metal strip hot at once, so all four pins should fall together.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Gives I, II, III, IV without explaining conduction or wax timing.
Names heat transfer but does not distinguish conduction from convection.
Uses pin distance but does not anchor the order to the flame-heated end.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Choose materials for cooking, drinking, clothing, or house walls by deciding whether easy heat flow or reduced heat flow is needed.
units.mechanism: Materials that allow heat to pass through them easily are good conductors; materials that do not allow heat to pass through easily are poor conductors or insulators.

mx.cwo: Use a wooden cooking utensil and a metal cup for tea because wood conducts heat to food and metal stops tea from losing heat.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Materials that allow heat to pass through them easily are good conductors; materials that do not allow heat to pass through easily are poor conductors or insulators.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A metal cup will keep tea hot longest because metal is sturdy, while material choice is not about heat flow.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names metal, clay, porcelain, wool, or hollow bricks without explaining heat flow.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: When air or water is heated from below, decide that the heated fluid expands, becomes lighter, rises, and cooler fluid moves down to replace it.
units.mechanism: In liquids and gases, heat transfer can take place by the actual movement of particles from one place to another; heated fluid expands, becomes lighter, rises, and cooler fluid moves down.

mx.cwo: The coloured streak rises in the middle, but no cooler water moves down from the sides to replace it.
Cooler water rises in the middle while hotter, lighter water sinks down the sides.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: In liquids and gases, heat transfer can take place by the actual movement of particles from one place to another; heated fluid expands, becomes lighter, rises, and cooler fluid moves down.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Heating water only warms the bottom layer; the rest of the beaker becomes hot without water actually moving.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names convection for the beaker activity without the motion sequence.
Says the coloured streak rises in the middle, matching H003_MX01 surface.
Mentions hot and cool water but may use the H003_MX02 reversal.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Identify conduction, convection, or radiation from what carries heat in the situation.
units.mechanism: Conduction transfers heat by contact from particle to particle, convection transfers heat by the actual movement of liquid or gas particles, and radiation transfers heat directly from a hot object to its surroundings.

mx.cwo: Flame to utensil is radiation, water heating is conduction, and warmth felt near the hot pan is convection.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Conduction transfers heat by contact from particle to particle, convection transfers heat by the actual movement of liquid or gas particles, and radiation transfers heat directly from a hot object to its surroundings.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Any heat coming from a flame is called radiation, no matter whether it warms a pan, water, or a person.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names conduction, convection, and radiation once.
Calls flame-related heat radiation.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Use the faster heating and cooling of land than water to decide the direction of daytime sea breeze and nighttime land breeze.
units.mechanism: Soil heats up faster and cools down faster than water; air above the warmer surface rises, and cooler air moves in from the other surface.

mx.cwo: During the day, air moves from land to sea; at night, air moves from sea to land.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Soil heats up faster and cools down faster than water; air above the warmer surface rises, and cooler air moves in from the other surface.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Wind near the coast always blows from the same direction because the sea is always cooler than land.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names sea breeze and land breeze without explaining warmer surface or rising air.
Gives a reversing pattern but may match the H005_MX01 wrong output.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide when heat reaches a person or object by radiation rather than by touch or moving fluid.
units.mechanism: Radiation transfers heat directly from a hot object to other objects or surroundings; the Sun's heat and the warmth felt from a fire reach us by radiation, and hot objects cool by radiating heat.

mx.cwo: A hot utensil cools because the cooler surroundings radiate heat into the utensil.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Radiation transfers heat directly from a hot object to other objects or surroundings; the Sun's heat and the warmth felt from a fire reach us by radiation, and hot objects cool by radiating heat.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Heat can reach a person only by touching the hot object, so warmth near a fire is not heat transfer unless there is contact.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says radiation for warmth near fire without direction or boundary.
Mentions fire warmth but explains it only by being near or touching the source.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Choose light-coloured clothes in summer and dark-coloured clothes in winter by deciding whether the surface mostly reflects or absorbs heat.
units.mechanism: Light-coloured surfaces reflect most of the heat that falls on them, while dark surfaces absorb more heat.

mx.cwo: Wear dark-coloured clothes in summer and light-coloured clothes in winter because dark surfaces reflect more heat and light surfaces absorb more heat.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Light-coloured surfaces reflect most of the heat that falls on them, while dark surfaces absorb more heat.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Clothing colour only changes appearance, so white and dark clothes should feel the same in summer and winter.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Gives the correct summer and winter colours without saying reflect or absorb.
Uses reflect and absorb but pairs dark with reflection or light with absorption.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Sequence the water cycle as Sun-driven evaporation and transpiration, rising and cooling of water vapour, condensation into clouds, precipitation, seepage or return flow, and return to water bodies.
units.mechanism: The Sun heats water in oceans, rivers, and lakes so it evaporates as water vapour; plants release water vapour through transpiration; rising vapour cools and condenses to form clouds, and clouds bring precipitation.

mx.cwo: Clouds evaporate to make water vapour, and water vapour then falls as rain before returning to oceans.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: The Sun heats water in oceans, rivers, and lakes so it evaporates as water vapour; plants release water vapour through transpiration; rising vapour cools and condenses to form clouds, and clouds bring precipitation.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Rain appears from clouds without evaporation from water bodies or transpiration from plants.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names evaporation, clouds, precipitation, and water bodies.
Gives Sun, vapour, clouds, and rain in order.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Predict which material lets water seep fastest by comparing the width and connection of spaces between its particles.
units.mechanism: Water seeps faster through materials with wider, open, connected spaces between particles; gravel lets water pass fastest, sand slower, and clay slowest.

mx.cwo: Clay lets water seep fastest, sand is slower, and gravel is slowest because narrow spaces speed water through.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Water seeps faster through materials with wider, open, connected spaces between particles; gravel lets water pass fastest, sand slower, and clay slowest.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Clay lets water pass fastest because its particles are finest and the surface looks smooth.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names a material order without explaining particle spaces.
