Says the tool makes things bigger but does not match tool to sample.
Uses clear-looking pond water to avoid selecting a tool.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a living organism should be understood as being built from cells, whether it has one cell or many cells.
units.mechanism: All living beings are made up of cells. A cell is the basic unit of life because one cell can be a whole unicellular organism, and many cells can build a multicellular organism.

mx.cwo: A chick is unicellular because it began as one egg cell.
Cells are made up of organisms, so the organism is the basic unit of a cell.
Only plants and animals are made of cells; bacteria and protozoa are not made of cells.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: All living beings are made up of cells. A cell is the basic unit of life because one cell can be a whole unicellular organism, and many cells can build a multicellular organism.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Only large plants and animals are made of cells; tiny bacteria are just specks, not cell-based organisms.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names unicellular or multicellular without cell reasoning.
Lists plant, human, bacterium, or Amoeba categories without the boundary check.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide which main cell part explains a job: cell membrane, cytoplasm, or nucleus.
units.mechanism: Cells have three main parts: the cell membrane, cytoplasm, and nucleus. The cell membrane encloses the cytoplasm and nucleus, separates cells, and allows useful materials in and wastes out; the cytoplasm contains cell components and many life processes occur there; the nucleus regulates cell activities and growth.

mx.cwo: The nucleus lets food enter and waste leave, while the cell membrane controls growth.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Cells have three main parts: the cell membrane, cytoplasm, and nucleus. The cell membrane encloses the cytoplasm and nucleus, separates cells, and allows useful materials in and wastes out; the cytoplasm contains cell components and many life processes occur there; the nucleus regulates cell activities and growth.
pedagogy.lok_folk: The nucleus is the important part, so it does every major job inside the cell.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names cell membrane, cytoplasm, and nucleus.
Uses the right vocabulary while reversing membrane and nucleus jobs.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide when firmness, green colour, or photosynthesis should be explained by cell wall, plastids, or chloroplasts rather than by the cell membrane alone.
units.mechanism: In plant cells, the cell wall provides rigidity and strength. Plant cells have plastids, and chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which makes them green and helps in photosynthesis. Fungal cells have a cell wall but do not have chloroplasts.

mx.cwo: The cell membrane gives plant cells rigidity, and the cell wall makes the green colour for photosynthesis.
Bread mould has a cell wall, so it must contain chloroplasts and make its own food by photosynthesis.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: In plant cells, the cell wall provides rigidity and strength. Plant cells have plastids, and chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which makes them green and helps in photosynthesis. Fungal cells have a cell wall but do not have chloroplasts.
pedagogy.lok_folk: The cell membrane is the outside covering, so it must explain firmness, green colour, and photosynthesis.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names cell wall, chloroplasts, and chlorophyll without assigning each function.
Uses the plant cell wall pattern to explain bread mould.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide how a cell's shape, size, and structure help it perform its specific function.
units.mechanism: The unique shape, size, and structure of cells help them carry out specific functions: thin flat cheek cells form a protective lining, elongated nerve cells carry messages, and muscle cells contract to help move food.

mx.cwo: Cheek cells carry messages because they are thin and flat, and nerve cells form the mouth lining because they are long and branched.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: The unique shape, size, and structure of cells help them carry out specific functions: thin flat cheek cells form a protective lining, elongated nerve cells carry messages, and muscle cells contract to help move food.
pedagogy.lok_folk: All animal cells do the same job because they are all cells from the same body.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Uses correct shape words but says cheek cells carry messages and neurons form the mouth lining.
Names cheek cells, neurons, and muscle cells without explaining how shape helps function.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide where a biological structure belongs in the sequence cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism.
units.mechanism: The levels of organisation in a living organism are ordered as Cell -> Tissue -> Organ -> Organ system -> Organism.

mx.cwo: Organism -> Organ system -> Organ -> Tissue -> Cell is the correct order because the whole body comes first.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: The levels of organisation in a living organism are ordered as Cell -> Tissue -> Organ -> Organ system -> Organism.
pedagogy.lok_folk: The biggest level should come first because the organism is what we can see.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names cell, tissue, organ, organ system, and organism.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether an organism with one cell or very few cells can still be a complete living organism.
units.mechanism: Some microorganisms, such as bacteria and protozoa, are unicellular organisms. They carry out all functions necessary for survival in a single cell, while multicellular organisms are made of many cells.

mx.cwo: A bacterium with one cell is not a complete organism because one cell cannot carry out all survival functions.
Multicellular organisms carry out all survival functions in a single cell, while unicellular organisms divide the work among many cells.
Only organisms with many cells are living organisms; one-celled microorganisms are non-living particles.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Some microorganisms, such as bacteria and protozoa, are unicellular organisms. They carry out all functions necessary for survival in a single cell, while multicellular organisms are made of many cells.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A real organism needs many parts and many cells, so one cell cannot be a whole living organism.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names unicellular but avoids whether one cell can be complete.
Uses tiny size to answer without checking living status.
Uses both terms but may assign the function pattern to the wrong group.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether tiny moving beings in pond water or soil suspension are microorganisms when they cannot be seen with the unaided eye.
units.mechanism: Microorganisms are very small living beings that cannot be seen with the naked or unaided eye. Pond water, stagnant water, and soil suspension can contain tiny organisms that become observable with a microscope or foldscope.

mx.cwo: If soil suspension contains microorganisms, they should be visible before using a microscope.
The moving speck in the soil suspension is just dirty soil because the drop looks muddy.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Microorganisms are very small living beings that cannot be seen with the naked or unaided eye. Pond water, stagnant water, and soil suspension can contain tiny organisms that become observable with a microscope or foldscope.
pedagogy.lok_folk: If water or soil only looks like dirt to my eye, any moving specks under a microscope are not living organisms.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says microorganisms without sample, unaided-eye limit, or magnification.
Mentions soil suspension but decides from muddy appearance.
Treats naked-eye invisibility as a decisive test.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide how to classify examples such as Amoeba, bread mould, bacteria, some algae, and viruses without treating all microscopic things as the same kind of organism.
units.mechanism: Microorganisms can be categorised into groups such as protozoa, fungi, bacteria, and some algae. Viruses are microscopic and acellular, and they multiply when they enter a living cell.

mx.cwo: Amoeba, bread mould, bacteria, algae, and viruses should all be classified as bacteria because all are microscopic.
Viruses are living cells that multiply first and then enter a living cell.
Bread mould is an alga because the growth on bread looks green.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Microorganisms can be categorised into groups such as protozoa, fungi, bacteria, and some algae. Viruses are microscopic and acellular, and they multiply when they enter a living cell.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Anything microscopic is basically a bacterium, so the exact category does not matter.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names protozoa, fungi, bacteria, algae, and virus without assigning examples.
Gives one label for bread mould or virus without checking the decisive feature or boundary.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide why some exposed foods rot while pickles and murabbas with enough salt or sugar do not get infected in the same way.
units.mechanism: Microorganisms can be found everywhere, including water, soil, air, surfaces, and some food items. Spices with high concentrations of salt or sugar act as preservatives because they do not allow these organisms to infect pickles and murabbas.

mx.cwo: Salt and sugar make microorganisms grow on pickles, so pickles get infected faster than a cut tomato.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Microorganisms can be found everywhere, including water, soil, air, surfaces, and some food items. Spices with high concentrations of salt or sugar act as preservatives because they do not allow these organisms to infect pickles and murabbas.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Pickles stay safe because they are pickles, while fresh foods rot because they are naturally weak.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Mentions microbes, salt, sugar, pickle, or murabba without the correct relation.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide how microorganisms can turn plant and animal waste into useful products and cleaner surroundings.
units.mechanism: Some soil microorganisms, especially fungi and bacteria, act on plant waste and slowly break it down into simpler nutrient-rich manure. Helpful bacteria can also decompose animal waste, and some microorganisms in oxygen-free environments decompose plant and animal waste as a source of biogas.

mx.cwo: Manure forms first and then creates fungi and bacteria; microbes are not needed to break down peels.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Some soil microorganisms, especially fungi and bacteria, act on plant waste and slowly break it down into simpler nutrient-rich manure. Helpful bacteria can also decompose animal waste, and some microorganisms in oxygen-free environments decompose plant and animal waste as a source of biogas.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Peels turn into manure just because they dry out in soil; microbes are not doing the work.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Mentions microorganisms, peels, and manure without saying who acts on what.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide why dough with yeast rises after some time while similar dough without yeast does not rise in the same way.
units.mechanism: Yeast is a microorganism belonging to fungi and grows well in warm conditions. When yeast is added to flour with sugar and warm water, the dough rises after some time; without yeast, the dough does not rise in the same way.

mx.cwo: Bowl B without yeast will rise more than bowl A because warm water alone makes the dough fluffy.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Yeast is a microorganism belonging to fungi and grows well in warm conditions. When yeast is added to flour with sugar and warm water, the dough rises after some time; without yeast, the dough does not rise in the same way.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Warm water and flour rise on their own; yeast powder is just a flavouring added to dough.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: States that bowl A rises but gives no yeast role or bowl B comparison.
Mentions warm water or warm place and time without naming yeast as the changed condition.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide why lukewarm milk with a curd starter forms curd while cold milk with the same starter does not curdle in the same way.
units.mechanism: When a small spoonful of curd is mixed into lukewarm milk and left for a few hours, the milk turns into curd and becomes a little sour. Cold milk with the same curd starter does not curdle in the same way, although it may become a little sour.

mx.cwo: Cold milk in bowl B will form curd, while lukewarm bowl A will only become slightly sour.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: When a small spoonful of curd is mixed into lukewarm milk and left for a few hours, the milk turns into curd and becomes a little sour. Cold milk with the same curd starter does not curdle in the same way, although it may become a little sour.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Any milk with a spoonful of curd will become curd equally fast, whether it is cold or lukewarm.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Mentions curd starter and sourness but avoids the temperature comparison.
Tracks both bowls but selects the wrong temperature direction.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide why conserving microalgae matters for the environment, oxygen balance, food security, and livelihoods.
units.mechanism: Microalgae are microscopic plant-like organisms that live in water, soil, air, and even on trees. They make their own food using sunlight, help maintain oxygen balance, and conserving them supports the environment, food security, and livelihood development.

mx.cwo: Microalgae only use oxygen and do not release it, so removing them would improve oxygen balance.
Conserving any microbe, including viruses, gives the same Spirulina-like food security and livelihood benefits.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Microalgae are microscopic plant-like organisms that live in water, soil, air, and even on trees. They make their own food using sunlight, help maintain oxygen balance, and conserving them supports the environment, food security, and livelihood development.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Microalgae are just pond scum, so losing them would not affect oxygen, food, or people.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says conserving tiny living things is good without naming chapter mechanisms.
Mentions oxygen but says microalgae only use it.
Mentions Spirulina and food benefits but applies them to all microbes or viruses.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether health is present by checking physical, mental, and social well-being, not only by checking for disease.
units.mechanism: Health is complete physical, mental, and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease.

mx.cwo: The moved-school student is fully healthy because he has no diagnosed disease, even though he is lonely, losing weight, and sleeping poorly.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Health is complete physical, mental, and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A person with no named disease is healthy, even if the person is lonely and cannot sleep well.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says physical, mental, and social well-being but still calls the student healthy.
Lists headaches and weight loss without using the health boundary.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide which daily habits and surroundings support health by linking food, hygiene, activity, sleep, stress, relationships, and cleanliness to body and mind.
units.mechanism: Healthy habits and clean surroundings support a healthy body and a healthy mind.

mx.cwo: Plan B is healthier because fast food gives quick energy and the dirty playground still lets students play outside.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Healthy habits and clean surroundings support a healthy body and a healthy mind.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Being healthy mainly means eating enough food, so junk food and a dirty playground do not matter if the student feels active.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Learner names a healthier plan without reasons.
Learner says outdoor play makes Plan B healthy.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Infer that a person is unwell when symptoms or signs show that the body or mind is not working normally.
units.mechanism: Being unwell means something in the body or mind may not be working as it should; a disease affects the normal working of the body or mind.

mx.cwo: Pain, dizziness, fever, and rash mean the body is working normally, so the person is well.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Being unwell means something in the body or mind may not be working as it should; a disease affects the normal working of the body or mind.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A person is unwell only when the discomfort is severe; fever, rash, pain, or dizziness can be ignored if the person keeps working.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Lists pain, dizziness, fever, and rash.
Names the clues but says they mean the body is working normally.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Classify a disease as communicable, non-communicable, or chronic from its cause, spread, and duration.
units.mechanism: Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens and can spread; non-communicable diseases are not caused by pathogens and do not spread from one person to another; chronic diseases persist for a long time, more than 3 months.

mx.cwo: Typhoid is non-communicable because pathogens cause it, and diabetes is communicable because lifestyle factors spread between people.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens and can spread; non-communicable diseases are not caused by pathogens and do not spread from one person to another; chronic diseases persist for a long time, more than 3 months.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Any serious or long-lasting disease must be communicable, and any disease with a germ word must be non-communicable because germs are inside the body.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Learner names communicable, non-communicable, or chronic without explaining the cue.
Learner recognizes typhoid or diabetes but cannot justify the label.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Choose prevention steps for a communicable disease by tracing how its pathogen spreads.
units.mechanism: Communicable diseases spread when pathogens move through routes such as air, contaminated food or water, direct or indirect contact, insects, or contact with a rabid animal; prevention blocks those routes.

mx.cwo: For a disease spreading through contaminated drinking water, washing hands once is enough; the food and water do not need to be kept clean.
For a mosquito-spread disease, the best prevention is only covering the mouth while coughing.
During a flu outbreak, sharing towels and sitting close to a coughing student will minimise spread.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Communicable diseases spread when pathogens move through routes such as air, contaminated food or water, direct or indirect contact, insects, or contact with a rabid animal; prevention blocks those routes.
pedagogy.lok_folk: One prevention step, such as washing hands, works the same way for every communicable disease route.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Mentions handwashing and cleanliness.
Names a real prevention step.
Mentions flu and contact actions.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Explain non-communicable disease risk and control through lifestyle, diet, environment, early diagnosis, and continuous care.
units.mechanism: Non-communicable diseases are usually linked to lifestyle, diet, and environment, and their control focuses on managing symptoms and improving quality of life through medication, lifestyle changes, rehabilitation, early diagnosis, and continuous care.

mx.cwo: Diabetes spreads from one student to another, so the main control is keeping the student away from friends; lifestyle changes and continuous care are not needed.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Non-communicable diseases are usually linked to lifestyle, diet, and environment, and their control focuses on managing symptoms and improving quality of life through medication, lifestyle changes, rehabilitation, early diagnosis, and continuous care.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A disease becomes controllable when the sick person is kept away from others for a few days.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Learner writes 'diabetes is non-communicable' but gives no risk or care explanation.
Learner sounds preventive by saying the student should avoid classmates.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Predict how immunity and vaccination reduce serious infections and their spread.
units.mechanism: Immunity is the body's ability to fight disease, and vaccines help the immune system develop protection against serious infections.

mx.cwo: A vaccinated student is more likely to get severe measles on later exposure because the immune response becomes weaker after vaccination.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Immunity is the body's ability to fight disease, and vaccines help the immune system develop protection against serious infections.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Vaccines are medicines taken after someone is sick, so they cure the disease rather than prepare the immune system.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says vaccines help people but gives no immune training or later-exposure prediction.
Says vaccines prevent disease while claiming the later response gets weaker.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide when antibiotics are suitable and why careless use can make bacterial infections harder to treat.
units.mechanism: Antibiotics kill bacteria that cause disease, but indiscriminate use can lead to antibiotic-resistant bacteria and reduce antibiotic effectiveness.

mx.cwo: Taking antibiotics whenever you have a sore throat and fever keeps antibiotics stronger and prevents resistant bacteria.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Antibiotics kill bacteria that cause disease, but indiscriminate use can lead to antibiotic-resistant bacteria and reduce antibiotic effectiveness.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Antibiotics are strong medicines for any fever or sore throat, and taking them often keeps them powerful.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Mentions antibiotics and bacteria without deciding when use is suitable.
Says sore throat and fever need antibiotics because frequent use keeps them strong.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Predict whether a nearby compass needle should deflect when electric current flows through a conductor.
units.mechanism: An electric current flowing through a conductor produces a magnetic field around it; when the current stops, the magnetic field disappears.

mx.cwo: With the switch OFF, the compass needle will still remain deflected near the wire.
The compass needle should deflect only after the wire is touched or heated, not simply when current flows through the nearby wire.
The compass needle deflects first, and that deflection produces the electric current in the wire.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: An electric current flowing through a conductor produces a magnetic field around it; when the current stops, the magnetic field disappears.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A compass needle moves only near a permanent magnet, so a wire connected to a cell should not move it.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says deflection occurs but does not separate switch ON from OFF.
Mentions warming or touching the wire while avoiding current-flow cause.
Uses current and compass words without saying which causes which.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a current-carrying coil is acting as a temporary magnet and whether an iron nail core makes it stronger.
units.mechanism: A current-carrying coil behaves like a magnet, and placing an iron nail in the coil makes the electromagnet stronger.

mx.cwo: Because the coil deflects a compass, the test is finished; inserting the iron nail cannot be used to compare the strength of the electromagnet.
The coil without the iron nail gives more compass deflection than the coil with the iron nail inside.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: A current-carrying coil behaves like a magnet, and placing an iron nail in the coil makes the electromagnet stronger.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Wrapping wire around a nail makes the nail a permanent magnet whether or not current is flowing.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says the coil deflects a compass.
Compares both setups but may choose the coil without nail.
Uses the word electromagnet without current or stop-current claims.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Identify the North and South poles of an electromagnet using a magnetic compass.
units.mechanism: An electromagnet has two poles, North and South; if the north pole of a compass is attracted to one end of the electromagnet, that end is the South pole and the other end has the opposite polarity.

mx.cwo: End A is South even when the coil is disconnected from the cell.
If the compass needle moves near end A, label end A as North without checking whether the compass north pole was attracted or repelled.
If the compass north pole is attracted to end A, end A is North and end B is South.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: An electromagnet has two poles, North and South; if the north pole of a compass is attracted to one end of the electromagnet, that end is the South pole and the other end has the opposite polarity.
pedagogy.lok_folk: If the compass north pole points toward an end, that end must also be North.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Gives A South and B North without condition or rule.
Mentions compass deflection but not which compass pole is attracted.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Predict whether a lifting electromagnet will pick up or release iron objects when the current is switched ON or OFF.
units.mechanism: A lifting electromagnet lifts iron objects while current is ON and releases them when current is switched OFF.

mx.cwo: Switch OFF makes the electromagnet pick up the paper clips; switch ON releases them.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: A lifting electromagnet lifts iron objects while current is ON and releases them when current is switched OFF.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Once the electromagnet has picked up clips, it should keep holding them until they are pulled off by hand.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Mentions pick up and release but not which switch state causes each.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Explain why a current-carrying wire such as nichrome becomes warm.
units.mechanism: When electric current flows through a conductor, resistance to the flow produces heat; different conducting materials can produce different amounts of heat.

mx.cwo: The nichrome wire must first become warm, and that warmth then makes electric current flow through the circuit.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: When electric current flows through a conductor, resistance to the flow produces heat; different conducting materials can produce different amounts of heat.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A wire becomes warm simply because the cell is connected, not because current meets resistance in the wire.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Sounds causal because it mentions warmth and current.
Mentions nichrome, current, and warm without a mechanism.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Compare how much heating occurs when the same wire is connected to one cell or two cells for the same duration, and judge whether that heating is useful or harmful in a situation.
units.mechanism: For the same wire and duration, using two cells generates more heat than using one cell; the heating effect is useful in appliances but unwanted overheating can damage plugs, sockets, and appliances.

mx.cwo: Two cells always produce more heat than one cell, even if the wire or heating time is changed between the two trials.
For the same wire and 30 s, one cell heats the wire more than two cells.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: For the same wire and duration, using two cells generates more heat than using one cell; the heating effect is useful in appliances but unwanted overheating can damage plugs, sockets, and appliances.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Any heating by electricity is useful, so more cells and hotter wires are always better.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says two cells heat more without checking same wire and duration.
Mentions same wire and 30 s but may select the wrong hotter setup.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Identify whether a setup is a working Voltaic cell by checking for two different metal electrodes and an electrolyte.
units.mechanism: A Voltaic cell uses two electrodes made of different materials and an electrolyte; the electrolyte helps conduct electricity between the electrodes, and a glowing LED shows that the cell is working.

mx.cwo: An iron nail and copper strip in pure water will light the LED when the switch is closed.
The LED makes electricity first, and that electricity turns the copper strip and iron nail in lemon juice into a working Voltaic cell.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: A Voltaic cell uses two electrodes made of different materials and an electrolyte; the electrolyte helps conduct electricity between the electrodes, and a glowing LED shows that the cell is working.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Putting any two objects into a lemon should make a battery because lemons are electric.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names copper and iron as different electrodes.
Mentions LED glow and electricity.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Classify an electric cell as a dry cell rather than a Voltaic cell from how its electrolyte is held and how convenient it is for everyday use.
units.mechanism: A dry cell has an electrolyte that is not a free liquid, making it more convenient for everyday use than a Voltaic cell with a liquid electrolyte.

mx.cwo: Voltaic cells are more convenient for everyday use because their electrolyte is a liquid.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: A dry cell has an electrolyte that is not a free liquid, making it more convenient for everyday use than a Voltaic cell with a liquid electrolyte.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A dry cell has no electrolyte at all because dry means completely dry inside.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Selects dry cell without naming paste-like electrolyte or convenience.
Mentions electrolyte but uses the Voltaic-liquid convenience claim.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Classify a battery as rechargeable rather than single-use by whether it can be recharged and reused multiple times.
units.mechanism: Rechargeable batteries can be recharged and reused multiple times, unlike dry cells that are single-use.

mx.cwo: A phone lithium-ion battery can be reused after it stops supplying electricity without charging it again.
A used-up dry cell should be recharged and reused, while a phone lithium-ion battery should be discarded after one use.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Rechargeable batteries can be recharged and reused multiple times, unlike dry cells that are single-use.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Any battery can be charged again if it is put into a charger for long enough.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says the phone Li-ion battery is rechargeable.
Correctly says one battery can be used again.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether an observed push or pull is a force and identify the interacting objects involved.
units.mechanism: A force is a push or pull on an object resulting from the object's interaction with another object; the SI unit of force is newton (N).

mx.cwo: When a hand pushes a table, the table applies the push on the hand, not the hand on the table.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: A force is a push or pull on an object resulting from the object's interaction with another object; the SI unit of force is newton (N).
pedagogy.lok_folk: Any visible movement is a force, so the interacting objects and the unit newton do not matter.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says force is present for the hand-table push.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide what effect an applied force can have on an object's motion or shape.
units.mechanism: A force applied on an object may make it move from rest, change its speed, change its direction of motion, change its shape, or cause several of these effects together.

mx.cwo: Pressing an inflated balloon has no force effect because the balloon stays in the same place.
The moving ball changes direction first, and that direction change creates the push from the bat.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: A force applied on an object may make it move from rest, change its speed, change its direction of motion, change its shape, or cause several of these effects together.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A force only counts when an object starts moving from rest.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Lists force-effect words without tying them to the three cases.
Gets bicycle or ball cases right but says the balloon has no force effect.
Names ball direction change but omits which event causes it.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether an object at rest must have no force acting on it.
units.mechanism: An object being at rest does not mean that no force acts on it; the forces acting on the object may be balancing one another.

mx.cwo: A book lying still on a table has 0 N of force acting on it because it is not moving.
The book becomes balanced because it is already at rest; rest makes the forces balance.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: An object being at rest does not mean that no force acts on it; the forces acting on the object may be balancing one another.
pedagogy.lok_folk: If an object is not moving, no force can be acting on it.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says 'no' without explaining why rest does not prove zero force.
Uses the words 'balanced forces' while saying rest makes balance happen.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Classify a force as contact or non-contact from how it acts between objects.
units.mechanism: Contact forces need physical contact between objects, while non-contact forces can be experienced even when the objects are not in contact. Muscular force and friction are contact forces; magnetic, electrostatic, and gravitational forces are non-contact forces.

mx.cwo: Magnetic force is a contact force because magnets push or pull, while friction is non-contact because no hand touches the rolling ball.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Contact forces need physical contact between objects, while non-contact forces can be experienced even when the objects are not in contact. Muscular force and friction are contact forces; magnetic, electrostatic, and gravitational forces are non-contact forces.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Contact force means a person touches the object, and non-contact force means no force is really present.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Repeats contact and non-contact labels without applying the rule to each force.
Uses push, pull, or stopping motion as if that classified the force.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide how friction affects a moving object and why rougher surfaces change the motion more.
units.mechanism: Friction acts between surfaces in contact and opposes the motion of the object; it arises due to irregularities in the two surfaces, and it is greater on rough surfaces.

mx.cwo: On sand the lunch box travels farther than on glass because rough surfaces make friction smaller.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Friction acts between surfaces in contact and opposes the motion of the object; it arises due to irregularities in the two surfaces, and it is greater on rough surfaces.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Friction appears only after the object has already stopped, so it does not oppose motion while the object moves.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names sand or friction without explaining direction or roughness.
Uses the word friction while leaving greater versus smaller friction unclear.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Identify magnetic force as a force that acts without contact on magnets or magnetic materials.
units.mechanism: A magnet can exert a force on another magnet or on a magnetic material without being in contact with it; this force is called magnetic force.

mx.cwo: The wooden stick in the ring-magnet setup is pulled by magnetic force because it is near the magnets.
A magnet can exert force on another magnet only after the two magnets touch, so the floating upper ring magnet has no magnetic force from the lower magnet.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: A magnet can exert a force on another magnet or on a magnetic material without being in contact with it; this force is called magnetic force.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A magnet only works by touching objects, and any object near a magnet is magnetic.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: says magnetic force
mentions an object near magnets
connects force with touching

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Predict attraction or repulsion from static electric charges.
units.mechanism: When certain materials are rubbed together, static charges build up on their surfaces. A charged body can exert electrostatic force on another charged body or on an uncharged body; like charges repel and unlike charges attract.

mx.cwo: Two similarly charged rubbed balloons attract each other, and a rubbed balloon and the woollen cloth repel each other.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: When certain materials are rubbed together, static charges build up on their surfaces. A charged body can exert electrostatic force on another charged body or on an uncharged body; like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Rubbing makes charged objects sticky, so all charged objects attract every nearby object in the same way.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Uses chapter objects but gives the H007_MX01 swapped outcomes.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Explain the motion of objects thrown upward or dropped using Earth's gravitational pull.
units.mechanism: Earth attracts objects towards itself with gravitational force. This force acts without contact and is always attractive; an object thrown upward slows down, stops momentarily, changes direction, and then speeds up while coming down.

mx.cwo: A ball thrown upward speeds up while going up because Earth pulls it upward until it reaches the top.
If the ball is thrown upward hard enough, Earth stops pulling it and it will not fall back down.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Earth attracts objects towards itself with gravitational force. This force acts without contact and is always attractive; an object thrown upward slows down, stops momentarily, changes direction, and then speeds up while coming down.
pedagogy.lok_folk: An object thrown upward carries an upward force from the throw until that force runs out, and Earth only pulls once it starts falling.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names gravity but avoids force direction and speed sequence.
Answers the first throw but ignores whether Earth still pulls when thrown harder.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Identify weight as the Earth's pull on an object and choose the correct unit.
units.mechanism: The weight of an object is the force with which the Earth pulls the object towards itself; weight measures how strongly the object is pulled by the Earth and is measured in newtons.

mx.cwo: Earth pulls a 5 N object because its weight is 5 N; the weight causes the Earth pull.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: The weight of an object is the force with which the Earth pulls the object towards itself; weight measures how strongly the object is pulled by the Earth and is measured in newtons.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Weight is the amount of matter in an object, so it should be written in kilograms even in science.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Answers newton without explaining Earth pull or force.
Says weight but not what defines it.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Calculate the smallest readable value of a spring balance from its scale divisions.
units.mechanism: For a spring balance, the smallest readable value is found by dividing the weight difference between two bigger marks by the number of small divisions between them; in the shown example, 1 N divided by 5 gives 0.2 N.

mx.cwo: 1 N + 5 divisions = 6 N, so one small division reads 6 N.
Because one small division is 0.2 N and there are 5 divisions, the two bigger marks are 0.04 N apart.
The smallest readable value is 10 N because the spring balance range is 0 to 10 N.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: For a spring balance, the smallest readable value is found by dividing the weight difference between two bigger marks by the number of small divisions between them; in the shown example, 1 N divided by 5 gives 0.2 N.
pedagogy.lok_folk: The smallest readable value is whichever number on the spring balance looks largest or most prominent.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Gives 0.2 N without showing interval or division count.
Mentions the 0 to 10 N range as if it proves the answer.
Uses 0.2 N and 5 but may reverse their roles.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Distinguish mass from weight when location or planet changes.
units.mechanism: Mass is the amount of matter in an object and is measured in grams or kilograms; its value remains the same at every place. Weight depends on gravitational force, so an object's weight can be different on different planets even when its mass remains the same.

mx.cwo: A 1 kg object has mass 25.4 kg on Jupiter because the table lists 25.4 N there.
The 1 kg object has the same 10 N weight on Earth, Moon, Mars, Venus, and Jupiter because its mass remains the same.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Mass is the amount of matter in an object and is measured in grams or kilograms; its value remains the same at every place. Weight depends on gravitational force, so an object's weight can be different on different planets even when its mass remains the same.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Mass and weight are two words for the same number, so changing planet should not change either one.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says one value stays same and one changes without kg or N.
Copies 25.4 for Jupiter without naming mass or weight.
Keeps 1 kg correct but claims 10 N weight everywhere.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Explain why an immersed object can feel lighter, float, or bounce upward in water.
units.mechanism: All liquids apply an upward force on immersed objects. When an object is fully or partially immersed in a liquid, it experiences an upward force equal to the weight of the liquid it displaces.

mx.cwo: A closed empty bottle bounces up in water because Earth pulls it upward through the water.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: All liquids apply an upward force on immersed objects. When an object is fully or partially immersed in a liquid, it experiences an upward force equal to the weight of the liquid it displaces.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Water removes gravity from immersed objects, so floating objects have no downward force on them.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names buoyant force or bounce upward without saying water applies the force.
Predicts the bottle bounces upward but uses the wrong output that Earth pulls it upward.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide how the pressure from a solid contact changes when the perpendicular force or the area of contact changes.
units.mechanism: For a force acting perpendicular to a surface, pressure is force per unit area; for the same force, a smaller area gives higher pressure and a larger area gives lower pressure.

mx.cwo: The narrow and broad bag straps give the same pressure because both bags have the same weight.
A broad bag strap gives more pressure than a narrow strap for the same bag.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner calculates pressure as perpendicular force divided by contact area and predicts that the same force gives higher pressure on a smaller area.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A heavier-feeling bag strap always means the bag has more weight, so the strap width is not part of the pressure explanation.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says Pressure = Force / Area but gives no calculation or strap comparison.
Uses equal bag weight to sound relevant.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether liquid pressure at a bottom point or tap depends on the height of liquid above the point rather than the total amount of water in the container.
units.mechanism: In a vertical liquid column, pressure at the bottom increases as the height of the liquid column increases; equal heights of the same liquid produce equal pressure even when the columns have different diameters.

mx.cwo: Adding more water to the pipe makes the balloon bulge less.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner predicts bottom or tap pressure from liquid column height, not from the total water amount or pipe diameter.
pedagogy.lok_folk: The tap with the most water stored above it always has the strongest stream, even if the water level height is the same.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says pressure depends on height but does not compare equal-height pipes or direction.
Says more water means more pressure, which can sound correct only when height also rises.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a fluid in a container exerts pressure only downward or also on the side walls.
units.mechanism: Liquids and gases exert pressure on the walls of their containers; water flows out through side holes because liquid pressure pushes on the side walls, and air inflates a balloon because it pushes outward on the balloon wall.

mx.cwo: The side holes do not show liquid pressure unless they are at the bottom of the bottle.
Water flows from the side holes because the bottle wall pushes the water outward, not because water pressure pushes on the wall.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner identifies that liquids and gases exert pressure on container walls as well as at the bottom.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Pressure in a fluid is just the weight pushing straight down on the bottom of the container.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: says liquids exert pressure in all directions
mentions side holes but not whether water or wall causes the push

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide when an effect is caused by atmospheric pressure acting over an area or by a pressure difference across an object.
units.mechanism: Atmospheric air surrounds the Earth and exerts pressure; when air pressure is lower inside a sealed space than outside, the higher outside pressure pushes the object against the surface.

mx.cwo: A rubber sucker sticks to a smooth surface because the smooth surface and rubber grip each other, even without lower pressure inside the cup.
A rubber sucker sticks because the air pressure inside the cup is higher than the air pressure outside it.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner explains atmospheric-pressure effects through outside air pressure over an area and pressure differences across an object.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Air is too light to press strongly, so a rubber sucker sticks mainly because rubber is sticky.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Mentions atmospheric pressure but gives no higher-lower comparison.
Mentions smooth surface and rubber sticking.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide the direction and speed of air flow from a pressure difference.
units.mechanism: Air flows from a region of higher pressure to a region of lower pressure; the flow continues until the pressures become almost equal, and a larger pressure difference gives faster air flow.

mx.cwo: Air moves from the uninflated balloon into the inflated balloon.
Air keeps flowing through the straw after both balloons become almost the same size.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner predicts that air flows from higher pressure to lower pressure and that a larger pressure difference produces faster flow.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Wind is moving air that chooses a direction by how hard it was first pushed, not by high and low air pressure regions.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: States pressure words but does not say when flow stops.
Chooses a balloon direction without identifying high and low pressure.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide how fast-moving air changes pressure around nearby objects and roofs.
units.mechanism: High-speed air is accompanied by lower pressure; higher pressure on nearby or opposite sides pushes objects toward the low-pressure region.

mx.cwo: Blowing harder between two balloons raises the pressure between them and pushes them apart.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner predicts lower pressure where air moves faster and uses the resulting pressure imbalance to explain motion or roof lift.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Faster wind always means stronger pressure in the place where the wind is moving fastest.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says balloons move together or a weak roof lifts without explaining pressure imbalance.
Mentions pressure but says faster air makes higher pressure in the gap.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide the chain by which heated land and moist air produce a thunderstorm.
units.mechanism: When land heats the warm moist air above it, the lighter air rises and creates a low-pressure area; cooler air from surrounding high-pressure areas flows in, warms, rises, cools, and its water vapour condenses into clouds and rain.

mx.cwo: Dry warm air rising above heated land forms rain clouds by itself.
Heated land makes warm moist air sink and create high pressure, so cooler surrounding air flows away from the land.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner explains thunderstorm formation as a chain from heated land to rising moist air, low pressure, inflow, cooling, condensation, clouds, and precipitation.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A thunderstorm happens simply because rain clouds get heavy and fall, without pressure-driven air circulation.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Uses heated land, air, clouds, and rain without explaining moisture.
Names pressure and cooler air but gives no flow direction.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide what sequence produces lightning and thunder inside or around storm clouds.
units.mechanism: Strong upward and downward winds cause water droplets and ice particles to rub and become charged; lighter positive ice particles collect higher in the cloud while heavier negative droplets collect lower, and a large charge buildup can break down air's insulation so charges suddenly flow as lightning.

mx.cwo: Thunder happens first; the sound causes charges to flow as lightning.
Any small rubbing of two cloud droplets immediately produces visible lightning.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner explains lightning and thunder through rubbing, charge separation, air-insulation breakdown, sudden discharge, and rapid heating and expansion of air.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Lightning is a bright flash made when clouds bump together, and thunder is the clouds crashing afterward.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names lightning, thunder, and charges without a causal order.
Says rubbing creates charges but skips the buildup threshold.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide how a warm-ocean storm becomes a cyclone and how the eye differs from the surrounding region.
units.mechanism: Cyclones are large storms that form over warm ocean waters; heated ocean water makes warm moist air rise, the water vapour condenses to raindrops, and the storm develops a lowest-pressure centre called the eye where winds are calm while surrounding regions have strong winds and heavy rainfall.

mx.cwo: The eye of a cyclone is where the strongest winds and heaviest rainfall occur.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner explains cyclone formation over warm ocean water and distinguishes the calm lowest-pressure eye from the surrounding strong winds and heavy rainfall.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A cyclone is just a very windy thunderstorm, and the centre must be the most dangerous part because it is the middle.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names cyclone, eye, or low pressure without locating calm wind versus strong wind and heavy rain.
Lists warm ocean and condensation but skips the eye-versus-surrounding comparison.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether breaking, grinding, or dissolving a substance shows that matter is made of extremely small particles rather than becoming nothing.
units.mechanism: Matter is composed of a large number of extremely small particles; even when a substance is finely powdered or dissolved, its particles can remain present though too small to see with ordinary observation.

mx.cwo: After grinding in the mortar, the chalk is no longer chalk; the fine white powder is a new substance.
When sugar grains disappear in water, there is 0 sugar left; the sweet taste is only water that changed taste.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner explains that grinding chalk or dissolving sugar changes size, visibility, or distribution while the substance remains present as extremely small constituent particles.
pedagogy.lok_folk: If no visible pieces of a substance remain, that substance has become nothing.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names particles but does not apply them to chalk or sugar.
Explains chalk correctly but says dissolved sugar is absent.
Accepts only visible specks as matter still present.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide where sugar goes when it dissolves in water and why the solution can taste sweet even when no sugar grains are visible.
units.mechanism: When sugar dissolves, tiny sugar particles separate and occupy available spaces between water particles, so sugar is present throughout the solution even though visible grains disappear.

mx.cwo: After stirring, the two teaspoons of sugar change into water, so the solution contains 0 sugar particles.
Water particles enter spaces inside the sugar grains, so the sugar stays as one invisible lump at the bottom.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner explains that dissolved sugar separates into tiny particles that occupy spaces between water particles, so sugar is still present throughout the solution.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Dissolved sugar has vanished because no sugar grains can be seen.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names interparticle spaces without saying sugar particles separate and spread.
Says the top tastes sweet but does not locate the sugar particles.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide why a solid has a definite shape and definite volume.
units.mechanism: In solids, particles are tightly packed and the interparticle attractions are very strong, so solids keep a definite shape and definite volume.

mx.cwo: A stone keeps its shape because its particles are far apart and the attractions between them are weak.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner explains definite shape and volume of solids by tightly packed particles, very strong interparticle attractions, and fixed positions with only vibration.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A solid keeps its shape only because its outside surface is hard.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says the object is a solid and has definite shape and volume.
Mentions particles and attraction but omits close or strong values.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide why heating a solid can make it melt and why the melting point is the temperature used to identify that change.
units.mechanism: When a solid is heated, its particles vibrate more vigorously until they can start leaving their positions; the minimum temperature at which a solid becomes a liquid at atmospheric pressure is its melting point.

mx.cwo: Ice melts at 0 degrees C because heating makes its particles vibrate less and the attractions become stronger.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner connects added heat to stronger particle vibrations, particles leaving fixed positions, and the solid becoming liquid at its melting point under atmospheric pressure.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Melting point is just a number in a table; heat changes state without a particle-motion reason.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names ice at 0 degrees C or urea at 133 degrees C.
Uses heat, vibrations, attraction, and melting point terms.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide why a liquid takes the shape of its container but still has a fixed volume.
units.mechanism: In liquids, particles can move and change positions within a limited space while remaining close enough under attraction, so liquids have no fixed shape but have a fixed volume.

mx.cwo: When 200 mL of water is poured into a wide container, it becomes 300 mL because liquids have no fixed shape.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner explains that liquid particles move and change positions within a limited space while attractions keep them close, so the liquid takes container shape but keeps its measured volume.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A liquid changes both shape and volume whenever its container changes.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says liquids take the shape of the container.
Mentions no fixed shape while predicting a changed amount.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide why a gas does not have a fixed shape or fixed volume.
units.mechanism: In gases, particles move freely in all directions and interparticle attractions are negligible, so gases spread to fill available space and have no fixed shape or fixed volume.

mx.cwo: Smoke fills Gas Jar B because gas particles strongly attract one another and pull the smoke into a fixed volume.
Smoke in Gas Jar A will fill Gas Jar B even while the glass plate stays in place and the jars are not connected.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner explains that gas particles move freely in all directions with negligible attractions, so gas spreads through available connected space and has no fixed shape or volume.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Gas is empty space, so smoke spreads by itself without needing moving air particles.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says gases have no fixed shape or volume.
Says smoke fills Gas Jar B.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide when a substance should be classified as a fluid rather than as a solid.
units.mechanism: Liquids and gases are fluids because they flow and do not retain a fixed shape; solids are distinguished from them by retaining a definite shape.

mx.cwo: Rice flour is a liquid because it pours into a jar and takes the jar's shape.
A key is a fluid because it keeps a definite shape, while water is not a fluid because it changes shape in a cup.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner classifies liquids and gases as fluids because they flow and lack fixed shape, while solids are not fluids merely because many grains can be poured.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Anything that can be poured is a liquid or fluid, even if it is made of many solid grains.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names water and air as fluids without giving the deciding property.
Uses takes-the-container-shape language for both water and rice flour.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide why air in a closed syringe can be compressed when the plunger is pushed.
units.mechanism: Gas can be compressed because there are large spaces between its particles; pushing the plunger forces the gas particles closer together and decreases the volume of air.

mx.cwo: In a closed syringe, pushing the plunger makes the air volume increase from 20 mL to 30 mL because particles move farther apart.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner explains that closing the syringe prevents escape and pushing the plunger decreases air volume by forcing gas particles closer together in their large interparticle spaces.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Compressed air must have leaked out, because the same gas cannot occupy a smaller volume.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says the air is compressed without saying why.
Mentions particles but not the direction of spacing change.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide why adding sugar and adding sand to water affect the mixture differently.
units.mechanism: Soluble sugar particles can become distributed in the spaces between water particles, so the water level may decrease after dissolving; insoluble sand does not dissolve, settles down, occupies space, and increases the total volume.

mx.cwo: After stirring, both two teaspoons of sugar and two teaspoons of sand dissolve, and both water levels fall below mark B.
Sugar settles at the bottom and raises the total volume, while sand particles fit between water particles and lower the level.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner compares soluble sugar with insoluble sand: dissolved sugar particles occupy spaces between water particles and may lower the level after mark B, while sand settles, occupies space, and increases total volume.
pedagogy.lok_folk: All small solids added to water behave the same once they are stirred.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names sugar as soluble and sand as insoluble.
Uses level language while saying both dissolve or swapping the solids.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide why colour or fragrance spreads through a liquid or gas, and how temperature changes the rate of spreading in water.
units.mechanism: Particles of liquids and gases are in constant motion; moving water particles spread potassium permanganate through water, moving gas particles spread fragrance through air, and hotter water spreads the colour faster because its particles move faster.

mx.cwo: The pink colour spreads fastest in ice-cold water and slowest in hot water because heat slows water particles.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner predicts spreading of colour or fragrance from constant particle motion and predicts fastest colour spreading in hot water because hotter particles move faster.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Colour or fragrance spreads only when someone stirs, blows, or carries it across the space.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Uses the word diffusion or names hot water without explaining particles.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether a sample is a mixture by checking whether two or more substances are physically mixed while each component keeps its own properties.
units.mechanism: A mixture forms when two or more substances are mixed without a chemical reaction; the individual substances retain their properties and are called components.

mx.cwo: Sugar water is a mixture even if the sugar and water chemically react to form a new substance.
A mixture forms when the components lose their original properties after mixing.
Only clear liquid samples like sugar water can be mixtures; sprout salad is not a mixture.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: A mixture forms when two or more substances are mixed without a chemical reaction; the individual substances retain their properties and are called components.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A sample is a mixture only when it looks blended into one smooth material.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says both samples are mixtures.
Counts sugar and water as two starting substances.
Correctly accepts sugar water as a mixture.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Classify a mixture as uniform or non-uniform by deciding whether its components are spread evenly and can be seen separately.
units.mechanism: In a uniform mixture, the components are mixed so evenly that they cannot be seen separately even with a microscope; in a non-uniform mixture, the different components or uneven distribution can be observed.

mx.cwo: Sugar water is non-uniform because sugar and water are two different substances.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: In a uniform mixture, the components are mixed so evenly that they cannot be seen separately even with a microscope; in a non-uniform mixture, the different components or uneven distribution can be observed.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A mixture with more than one substance must be non-uniform because different substances are present.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names a mixture as uniform without giving the criterion.
Mentions sugar and water correctly but uses them to choose non-uniform.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide whether air is a mixture by using its several gas components and the fact that they are not chemically combined into one substance.
units.mechanism: Air is a uniform mixture made mainly of nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide, and water vapour; a mixture contains two or more substances mixed without undergoing a chemical change.

mx.cwo: Air is a pure substance because nitrogen makes up about 78 percent of air.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Air is a uniform mixture made mainly of nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide, and water vapour; a mixture contains two or more substances mixed without undergoing a chemical change.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Air is one substance because it looks invisible and uniform.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says air is a mixture with no named gases or mixture-definition warrant.
Mentions that nitrogen makes up about 78 percent of air.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Explain why lime water turns milky when exposed to air by identifying carbon dioxide as the reacting gas.
units.mechanism: Lime water turns milky when carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide to form insoluble tiny white particles of calcium carbonate and water.

mx.cwo: Lime water turns milky because calcium carbonate in air reacts to make carbon dioxide.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: Lime water turns milky when carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide to form insoluble tiny white particles of calcium carbonate and water.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Lime water turns milky because air makes clear water dirty.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: States that lime water turns milky when exposed to air.
Mentions calcium carbonate without saying whether it is reactant or product.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Apply the scientific meaning of pure substance instead of the everyday meaning of pure on consumer products.
units.mechanism: In science, a pure substance has no other substance present in it, consists of the same type of particles, and cannot be separated into other kinds of matter by a physical process.

mx.cwo: A packet of pure fruit juice is a pure substance in science because the label says pure.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly applies this rule: In science, a pure substance has no other substance present in it, consists of the same type of particles, and cannot be separated into other kinds of matter by a physical process.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Pure on a product label means the material is a pure substance in science.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Repeats that the fruit juice is pure because the packet says pure.

units.subject: science

units.decision_hinge: Decide when a new organism is produced by asexual reproduction or vegetative propagation rather than by seeds from two parents.
units.mechanism: In asexual reproduction, one parent produces new individuals that are exact copies in their cell instructions; in vegetative propagation, a new plant can grow from a leaf, stem, or root such as a money plant cutting, potato eye, or piece of ginger.

mx.cwo: A potato eye is produced by the new potato plant after it grows; the eye is not the starting plant part for reproduction.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly uses the chapter relationship: In asexual reproduction, one parent produces new individuals that are exact copies in their cell instructions; in vegetative propagation, a new plant can grow from a leaf, stem, or root such as a money plant cutting, potato eye, or piece of ginger.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Any new plant that grows from soil must have come from a seed and two parents.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says asexual reproduction for the plant-part cases without any source condition.
Names potato as an example but keeps the wrong output about the eye appearing after the plant.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide how sexual reproduction avoids doubling genetic instructions while still mixing information from two parents.
units.mechanism: Sexual reproduction involves two parents and specialised reproductive cells called gametes; each gamete carries half of a parent's genetic material, and joining male and female gametes forms a new cell with a complete mix of genetic information.

mx.cwo: A sperm and an egg each carry a full set of genetic material, so the baby gets two complete sets every generation.
The two parents body cells simply join directly; no specialised gametes are needed.
Gametes become half only after fertilisation, when the zygote divides the complete set into two halves.
Because babies get a mix from both parents, every brother and sister must look exactly 50 per cent like the mother and 50 per cent like the father.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly uses the chapter relationship: Sexual reproduction involves two parents and specialised reproductive cells called gametes; each gamete carries half of a parent's genetic material, and joining male and female gametes forms a new cell with a complete mix of genetic information.
pedagogy.lok_folk: A baby simply receives a full instruction manual from each parent, so the amount of genetic material doubles each generation.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Says gametes and fertilisation but not half-material.
Says both parents contribute but skips specialised gametes.
Says halves and joining but does not place halves before fertilisation.
Says mix from both parents but claims exact 50-50 appearance.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide where male and female gametes are found and how fertilisation happens in flowering plants and animals.
units.mechanism: In flowering plants, pollen grains inside the anther are male gametes and ovules inside the flower are female gametes; in animals, sperm are male gametes and eggs are female gametes, and fertilisation may occur in water or inside the female.

mx.cwo: In flowering plants, ovules in the anther are male gametes and pollen grains deep inside the flower are female gametes.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly uses the chapter relationship: In flowering plants, pollen grains inside the anther are male gametes and ovules inside the flower are female gametes; in animals, sperm are male gametes and eggs are female gametes, and fertilisation may occur in water or inside the female.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Pollen is just a powder on flowers and eggs are only bird eggs, so they are not gametes.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names pollen, ovules, sperm, and eggs without sex-location or setting checks.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide where a fertilised egg develops in birds compared with most mammals.
units.mechanism: In birds, the fertilised egg is laid and the zygote develops into an embryo during hatching; in most mammals, the zygote develops into an embryo inside the female body, where the mother's body supplies food and oxygen until birth.

mx.cwo: In birds the zygote develops inside the female until birth, while in most mammals the zygote is laid and develops during hatching.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly uses the chapter relationship: In birds, the fertilised egg is laid and the zygote develops into an embryo during hatching; in most mammals, the zygote develops into an embryo inside the female body, where the mother's body supplies food and oxygen until birth.
pedagogy.lok_folk: All animals develop fertilised eggs the same way once sperm reaches the egg.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names eggs and birth but does not assign the development locations.
Uses zygote, embryo, hatching, and female body in fluent prose.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide how human actions create major threats to life on Earth.
units.mechanism: Human actions disturb the balance of living and non-living systems; burning fossil fuels releases greenhouse gases that trap more heat and cause global warming, while habitat destruction, biodiversity loss, and pollution harm ecosystems and people.

mx.cwo: Global warming releases coal and oil from underground, so climate change causes fossil-fuel burning.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly uses the chapter relationship: Human actions disturb the balance of living and non-living systems; burning fossil fuels releases greenhouse gases that trap more heat and cause global warming, while habitat destruction, biodiversity loss, and pollution harm ecosystems and people.
pedagogy.lok_folk: Environmental threats are separate problems, so burning fuels, habitat loss, and pollution do not affect the same life-supporting balance.

gaming_pockets.apparent_success: Names the triple planetary crisis without explaining how human actions create threats.
Mentions fossil fuels, greenhouse gases, and warming but may reverse the chain.

units.subject: science
units.decision_hinge: Decide why protecting life on Earth requires connected actions rather than one isolated fix.
units.mechanism: Because Earth's hydrosphere, biosphere, atmosphere, and geosphere are connected, protecting life requires cutting greenhouse gases and pollution, protecting biodiversity, using cleaner energy, and making responsible choices such as reusing, repairing, recycling, and saving energy and water.

mx.cwo: Protecting life only requires recycling plastic; cleaner energy, biodiversity, water, and community action are optional.
To protect the climate, people should use dirtier energy and make more pollution so communities have more to clean up.
Earth systems must first become balanced on their own; only then can people reuse, save energy, and work together.

pedagogy.mastery_signal: The learner correctly uses the chapter relationship: Because Earth's hydrosphere, biosphere, atmosphere, and geosphere are connected, protecting life requires cutting greenhouse gases and pollution, protecting biodiversity, using cleaner energy, and making responsible choices such as reusing, repairing, recycling, and saving energy and water.
pedagogy.lok_folk: One visible action, such as recycling plastic, is enough to protect all life-supporting systems on Earth.

uses protection words while choosing dirtier energy or more pollution
mentions balance and action but puts balance before responsible action
